title: Hidden Hearing Loss, Gene Therapy and Regeneration

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: An audiogram plots behavioural {{c1::threshold}} against sound frequency.
cards.back: Threshold is the quietest sound that evokes a response.
cards.quote: An audiogram plots behavioural threshold against frequency.

cards.front: An inner hair cell passes sound to auditory nerve fibres at a {{c1::ribbon synapse}}.
cards.back: The ribbon helps hold a ready supply of vesicles.
cards.quote: A ribbon synapse is the contact where an inner hair cell passes sound to auditory nerve fibres.

cards.front: How does transmitter release from an inner hair cell relate to its receptor potential?
cards.back: Release is continuous and graded with the receptor potential, the voltage change evoked by sound.
cards.quote: The cell releases transmitter continuously, graded with its receptor potential (its voltage change in response to sound).

cards.front: Loss of synapses between surviving hair cells and nerve fibres is called {{c1::cochlear synaptopathy}}.
cards.quote: Losing the synapses between hair cells and nerve fibres while the hair cells survive is called cochlear synaptopathy.
cards.section: A hearing test passed by a damaged cochlea

cards.front: In the Kujawa–Liberman noise experiment in male CBA/CaJ mice, what dissociation between threshold recovery and ribbon counts demonstrated concealed injury?
cards.back: Thresholds recovered by two weeks with intact hair cells, but ribbon counts at the 32 kHz place were about 50 percent below control at eight weeks.
cards.quote: At eight weeks the ribbon count in the 32 kHz region was about 50 percent below control,
cards.section: A hearing test passed by a damaged cochlea

cards.front: In hypothetical cochlear measurements, mean ribbons per inner hair cell fall from 18 to 10.8 after noise while thresholds return to baseline. What percentage was lost, and does threshold recovery exclude it?
cards.back: (18 − 10.8) / 18 × 100 = 40 percent lost. No: threshold recovery measures sensitivity and can coexist with substantial synapse loss.
cards.quote: It shows that recovered sensitivity can conceal injury,
cards.section: A hearing test passed by a damaged cochlea

cards.front: Why can a cochlea lose many synapses while retaining a near-normal threshold?
cards.back: Threshold depends mostly on the most sensitive fibres producing a detectable response above background. Enough can survive despite substantial loss elsewhere.
cards.quote: That depends mostly on the most sensitive fibres, and it does not count synapses.
cards.section: Why a threshold can miss half the synapses

cards.front: In the lesson’s illustrative fibre model, two otherwise identical auditory fibre populations each lose half their fibres. One loses the most sensitive half, the other the least sensitive half. Which threshold shifts more, and why?
cards.back: The population losing the most sensitive half has the larger upward shift. Those fibres normally detect the quietest sounds above background firing.
cards.quote: In the model, then, the threshold stays near normal while most of the sensitive fibres survive, and moves if they are the ones lost.
cards.section: Why a threshold can miss half the synapses

cards.front: Assume every auditory nerve fibre reaches the same sound-driven firing ceiling during a loud sound. Half the fibres are removed. What happens to the summed sound-driven response, and why?
cards.back: It falls to half the intact response: half as many fibres contribute the same per-fibre firing rate, regardless of which half survived.
cards.quote: The loud-sound response halves in every case, because at 80 dB every fibre is near the same ceiling.
cards.section: Why a threshold can miss half the synapses

cards.front: The earliest peak of the auditory brainstem response, {{c1::wave I}}, comes from the auditory nerve.
cards.back: The ABR is recorded electrically from the scalp after a sound.
cards.quote: and its earliest peak, wave I, comes from the auditory nerve.
cards.section: Why a threshold can miss half the synapses

cards.front: A fibre-count model predicts that a loud-sound response halves after fibre loss. Can this establish that human ABR wave I amplitude will halve? Explain the missing link.
cards.back: No. The model sums firing; wave I also depends on firing synchrony. The rule that lost fibres reduce the summed response does not specify their contribution to a synchronized electrical peak.
cards.quote: The model counts firing and does not compute wave I, which also depends on how synchronously the fibres fire.
cards.section: Why a threshold can miss half the synapses

cards.front: In electrocochleography, what is the main source of the summating potential (SP)?
cards.back: Hair cells; SP is mainly pre-neural, with some neural contribution.
cards.quote: The summating potential (SP) is mainly pre-neural. It comes largely from the hair cells, with some neural contribution.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: The auditory nerve compound action potential reflects the summed, {{c1::synchronized}} firing of many fibres.
cards.quote: the summed, synchronized firing of many fibres at once.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: A cochlear recording has a mainly hair-cell signal, SP, and a summed nerve signal, AP. Some AP-contributing fibres are lost while SP stays constant. What happens to SP/AP, and why?
cards.back: SP/AP rises because its denominator, AP, becomes smaller while SP remains constant.
cards.quote: If SP stays about the same and the lost fibres were contributing to AP, AP gets smaller and the ratio rises.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: Liberman’s human noise-risk comparison found a higher SP/AP ratio mainly from larger SP, without a significant AP decrease. Does this specifically identify neural loss?
cards.back: No. The proposed neural-loss interpretation predicts a smaller AP. A larger numerator can raise the same ratio without demonstrating that loss.
cards.quote: In the first study the ratio rose, but not for the reason the proxy assumes.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: Why did Guest’s negative ABR and envelope-following proxy results fail to rule out synaptopathy in adults with speech-in-noise difficulty?
cards.back: The proxies’ sensitivity to human synapse loss was unknown. A negative test cannot exclude a lesion it may fail to detect.
cards.quote: a negative result from a test of unknown sensitivity cannot rule the lesion out.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: What did postmortem temporal-bone counts contribute to the human noise-injury evidence, and what did they not count?
cards.back: They directly showed nerve fibre loss, worse with noise history. They did not count synapses.
cards.quote: These counts show nerve fibre loss directly, though they do not count synapses.
cards.section: Finding the lesion in people

cards.front: OTOF encodes {{c1::otoferlin}}, a protein with several C2 domains that often bind calcium.
cards.quote: its product is otoferlin, a protein with several C2 domains, modules that often bind calcium.
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: A depolarized inner hair cell has a normal calcium current but almost no membrane-capacitance rise. What process is impaired, and why does capacitance report it?
cards.back: Exocytosis is impaired downstream of calcium entry. Vesicle fusion adds membrane, so the capacitance rise tracks release.
cards.quote: The rise in membrane capacitance tracks how much vesicle membrane fuses, so it measures release.
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: In Otof-null mouse inner hair cells, calcium current and ribbon morphogenesis were preserved at the recorded age, but exocytosis was almost abolished. Where does this place the defect?
cards.back: Downstream of calcium entry. It establishes a release requirement for otoferlin without identifying the exact defective step.
cards.quote: That places the defect downstream of calcium entry, without naming the exact step.
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: Why does loss of release after otoferlin knockout not by itself prove that otoferlin is a calcium sensor?
cards.back: A required protein could dock or prime vesicles without sensing calcium. Necessity for release does not identify its mechanism.
cards.quote: a protein could be needed to dock or prime vesicles without sensing anything.
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: In a mouse, a C2C-domain otoferlin knock-in reduces calcium binding while retaining the protein. Fast and sustained exocytosis become less calcium-sensitive. Which mechanistic interpretation is supported, and what remains unproved?
cards.back: A calcium-sensing role is supported because altered binding changes release sensitivity while the protein remains present. It does not establish that otoferlin is the only sensor.
cards.quote: That fits a calcium-sensing role, and it does not show that otoferlin is the only sensor.
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: You want to distinguish otoferlin’s calcium-sensing role from a general requirement for release. What would a calcium-binding mutant add to a knockout, and what control matters?
cards.back: The knockout tests necessity. A binding mutant tests whether calcium-dependent release changes while otoferlin remains present; verify protein presence so loss of the protein cannot explain the result. This follows the C2C knock-in logic.
cards.quote: The protein was present, so its absence could not explain any change,
cards.section: The link that has to fire: what makes the synapse release

cards.front: Faint sounds generated by outer hair cell amplification are called {{c1::otoacoustic emissions (OAEs)}}.
cards.quote: Otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) are faint sounds the ear itself makes when the outer hair cells amplify.
cards.section: Putting the link back: a gene too big for its vector

cards.front: Why does full-length otoferlin gene replacement require more than one conventional AAV vector?
cards.back: Its coding sequence is about 6 kb before adding a promoter, exceeding one conventional AAV vector’s roughly 4.7 to 5 kb capacity.
cards.quote: The otoferlin coding sequence is about 6 kb, before a promoter is even added, so it cannot ride in one vector.
cards.section: Putting the link back: a gene too big for its vector

cards.front: In split-cDNA otoferlin delivery, what must an inner hair cell receive to rebuild the full-length gene cassette?
cards.back: Both vectors, each carrying part of the gene.
cards.quote: Each carries part of the gene, and a cell that receives both can join the parts back into the full-length cassette.
cards.section: Putting the link back: a gene too big for its vector

cards.front: In a hypothetical split-gene delivery experiment, vector A reaches 80 percent of cells and vector B reaches 60 percent, independently. Every cell receiving both expresses the full protein; no other cell does. What percentage expresses it?
cards.back: P(A and B) = 0.80 × 0.60 = 0.48, so 48 percent express the full protein. Independence allows multiplication; both halves are required.
cards.quote: Real transduction need not be independent, so this only shows why coverage is capped.
cards.section: Putting the link back: a gene too big for its vector

cards.front: After dual-vector treatment of neonatal Otof-null mice, fast exocytosis returned in transduced cells, but replenishment reached only 35 to 50 percent of wild type and click-ABR thresholds were 40 to 60 dB SPL. Is release rescue equivalent to normal hearing?
cards.back: No. Rescue was partial: fast release recovered, but replenishment and hearing did not normalize. Repairing one part of transmission did not restore the whole chain.
cards.quote: Click-evoked ABR thresholds in treated mice were 40 to 60 dB SPL, in mice that were deaf without treatment: better, but not normal hearing.
cards.section: Putting the link back: a gene too big for its vector

cards.front: What reference defines 0 dB HL, and how does dB SPL differ?
cards.back: 0 dB HL refers to average normal hearing. dB SPL uses a fixed sound-pressure reference.
cards.quote: dB HL is measured against average normal hearing, so 0 dB HL is average normal;
cards.section: Reading an early-phase trial without inflating it

cards.front: In the twelve-child DB-OTO report, nine met the week-24 endpoint of average threshold 70 dB HL or better, and three reached average normal sensitivity. Calculate each share and label it precisely.
cards.back: Endpoint: 9 / 12 × 100 = 75 percent. Average normal sensitivity: 3 / 12 × 100 = 25 percent. The endpoint rate is not the normal-hearing rate.
cards.quote: Nine of twelve met the week-24 primary endpoint, an average of 70 dB HL or better,
cards.section: Reading an early-phase trial without inflating it

cards.front: What durability conclusion follows from otoferlin gene-therapy follow-up lasting up to about two and a half years in some participants?
cards.back: Benefit persisted over the observed years in those participants. The reports do not establish lifelong durability.
cards.quote: which is evidence of persistence over those years and not proof of lifelong durability.
cards.section: Reading an early-phase trial without inflating it

cards.front: A hypothetical child’s baseline average ABR threshold is above a 100 dB test ceiling. The follow-up threshold is 65 dB on the same scale. What bound can be placed on the threshold improvement?
cards.back: Let baseline B > 100 dB. Improvement = B − 65 dB > 100 − 65 = 35 dB. It exceeds 35 dB; the exact improvement is unknown.
cards.quote: because the baseline was above the test ceiling and was not measured.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a censored number

cards.front: Why can a threshold improvement bounded by a test ceiling not be reported as a percentage of hearing restored by dividing the bound by that ceiling?
cards.back: The ceiling is not the measured baseline, and the bound is not the exact improvement. Their ratio does not identify a fraction of hearing restored.
cards.quote: These censored values do not identify a percentage of hearing restored.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a censored number

cards.front: Contrast natural hair-cell replacement in birds, zebrafish, and the adult mammalian cochlea, including the mammalian vestibular exception.
cards.back: Bird cochleas and the zebrafish lateral line replace hair cells. The adult mammalian cochlea does not; hair cells reappeared in damaged guinea-pig utricles, a vestibular organ.
cards.quote: Mammals do have one exception, and it is vestibular: after gentamicin damage, hair cells reappeared in guinea-pig utricles
cards.section: When the cell itself is gone: regeneration

cards.front: Two ears fail to transmit sound: one retains inner hair cells but lacks a functional release protein; the other has lost those cells. Would supplying the protein’s gene alone repair both? Explain.
cards.back: Only the ear with surviving cells could benefit from that replacement alone. The rule is to repair the missing link: absent hair cells require new cells and nerve connections, as well as functioning release machinery.
cards.quote: When noise, drugs or age kill the hair cells, there is no cell to put a gene back into,
cards.section: When the cell itself is gone: regeneration

cards.front: In mouse cochlear reprogramming, ATOH1-containing combinations worked at day 1, but by day 8 the three-factor combination was far more effective than simpler combinations. In untreated mice, hair-cell gene loci became less accessible with age. What barrier does this suggest?
cards.back: Age-dependent chromatin accessibility is a candidate barrier beyond simply lacking transcription factors. The profiling supports that hypothesis but does not alone prove the cause of reduced conversion.
cards.quote: Joint RNA and chromatin profiling of untreated mice showed hair-cell gene loci becoming less accessible between the two ages,
cards.section: When the cell itself is gone: regeneration

cards.front: What did lineage-traced reprogramming in mature mouse cochleas establish about new hair-cell-like cells, and what functional outcome remained unshown?
cards.back: Some supporting cells became hair-cell-like cells with rudimentary bundles, innervation and ribbon-synapse proteins. Functional transmission and restored hearing were not demonstrated.
cards.quote: but functional transmission through those contacts and restored hearing were not demonstrated.
cards.section: When the cell itself is gone: regeneration

cards.front: Reprogrammed cells in a deafened mature mouse cochlea have rudimentary bundles, nerve contacts and ribbon-synapse proteins. What functional tests would address the remaining gap to restored hearing?
cards.back: Record transmission between the new cells and spiral ganglion neurons, and measure auditory responses in the deafened mature animals. The chain rule requires working synapses and an auditory response beyond structural contacts.
cards.quote: which would be tested by recording from them and by measuring auditory responses in deafened mature animals.
cards.section: When the cell itself is gone: regeneration

cards.front: A study asks whether noise-related neural injury explains speech-in-noise complaints despite normal audiograms. How should it define the complaint and physiological proxy before analyzing their association?
cards.back: Prespecify the speech-in-noise test and endpoint, select the physiological proxy, and base sample size on its repeatability, variability and a stated effect size. The rule is to establish complaint, lesion and test separately; association cannot validate an insensitive proxy.
cards.quote: Fix the speech-in-noise test and its endpoint before looking at the proxy.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mouse noise exposure produces synapse loss despite recovered thresholds; some people report speech-in-noise difficulty despite normal audiograms. Does combining those observations establish a human diagnosis of noise synaptopathy?
cards.back: No. The mouse experiment supplies a lesion and timing, while the human observation supplies a complaint. The rule separates complaint, lesion and validated test: human prevalence, a diagnostic criterion and causation still require evidence.
cards.quote: the mouse noise experiment supplies the lesion and its timing, but not its prevalence in people, a diagnostic criterion,
cards.section: Design problem
